To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) molar and molecular movements are not mutually exclusive categories, but rather overlapping segmentations of the same processes; 2) the distinction between molar and molecular is not an ontological distinction, but rather an analytical distinction that allows for the study of how movements and political forces become molar or molecular; 3) the molar and molecular can be used to examine how movements and political processes become perceptible and impercepible, and thus how the political is made and unmade
The paper concludes by considering what the politics of perceptible/invisible movements might mean for political action and activism.

(1) The molar and the molecular are not opposed, but rather are tendencies or ‘segmentation’; (2) The politics of molar movements and affects are not necessarily the same, and the politics of molecular movements and affects may also be significant; (3) A focus on molecular movements and affects requires mobility scholars to move beyond binary thinking, and to think of the political in terms of the processes of becoming-molar and the becoming-molecular.

the politics of perceptible movements and the politics of imperceptible movements, which are often overlooked in mobility and migration studies.
